title_original: The Art Market Wanted to Go Global—It Didn’t Plan for Everything That Means
excerpt_original: The world outside the fairgrounds isn't always peaceful, predictable, or particularly interested in the needs of the art trade.

blocks.text: Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance , the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday. On the Saturday before the opening of Art Basel Paris , two art professionals I’m friendly with found themselves trapped in a Paris metro station. Protesters were stampeding down the stairs, trailed by clouds of tear gas. They couldn’t see, could barely breathe, and struggled to find their way out. When they finally emerged onto the street a block or two away, people were sitting in restaurants, eating and drinking as though nothing had happened.

The contrast is almost comical, though I doubt anyone caught in the tear gas was laughing. One minute, you’re wondering whether you’ll make it out of a subway station. The next, someone is ordering another glass of bordeaux.
A few days later, the rest of the art world got its own reminder that the world doesn’t particularly care about its calendar.

Art Basel Paris, which had opened for its ultra-exclusive Avant-Première event last Tuesday, closed Friday evening, two days ahead of schedule, as organizers braced for a second weekend of demonstrations. Protests over education spending and inequality had already turned into rioting and looting the previous Saturday. Now activists were threatening to converge on the Grand Palais itself, where dealers were offering paintings worth tens of millions of dollars.

Closing was the sensible decision. Nobody wants to explain to an insurance company how a seven-figure Gerhard Richter ended up in the middle of a riot. But the decision also raised an uncomfortable question: What happens when an international art market built on gathering wealthy people in expensive places runs into a world that isn’t always hospitable?
It’s a question the industry might want to get used to answering.

Earlier this year, I was in Madrid when news broke that drones were being intercepted over Dubai following joint US and Israeli strikes on Iran. My wife called to tell me that, whatever plans I had to attend Art Dubai , I wouldn’t be going. I called a friend in the city to see how things were. She was at the beach.

The art market has become very good at carrying on with business. Over the past three decades, it has grown into an enormous circuit of fairs, auctions, gallery openings, and biennials, supported by dealers, collectors, advisers, shippers, insurers, and people who seem to spend more time in airport lounges than at home.

For years, that growth was treated as an unqualified good. More fairs meant more collectors, more opportunities for galleries, and, at least in theory, a more international and democratic art market. But globalization works both ways. If you’re going to do business everywhere, you’re going to encounter everything that happens everywhere, too.

Art Basel Miami Beach was supposed to debut in December 2001, but the September 11 attacks forced organizers to postpone the inaugural edition until 2002. In 2015, Paris Photo closed early after the coordinated terrorist attacks across Paris, including at the Bataclan concert hall, that killed 130 people. And in March 2020, TEFAF Maastricht became one of the art world’s early Covid horror stories. The fair closed four days early after an exhibitor tested positive, and later reporting by The Art Newspaper identified more than 25 cases among attendees and exhibitors. Two years later, the fair was robbed .
Sometimes organizers decide the show must go on.

After devastating wildfires swept through Los Angeles in January 2025, Frieze insisted that its Los Angeles fair would go ahead in February, arguing that bringing collectors and galleries to the city would help support the local arts community. It was an understandable position, though there was something uncomfortable about an international art fair being presented as a community-building exercise while parts of the city were still recovering from disaster.

There’s no obvious rule for these situations. Cancel a fair, and galleries lose business. Hold it, and you risk appearing indifferent to what’s happening outside. Either way, someone’s going to be unhappy.

In Paris, some dealers I spoke to weren’t particularly bothered by the closure. They’d already made their sales during the VIP days and saw little reason to take unnecessary risks. Marc Payot , president of Hauser & Wirth, told the Financial Times that his gallery generally does most of its business early in the fair. But not everyone operates like Hauser & Wirth.

New York dealer Miguel Abreu told me that his gallery typically does about 20 percent of its fair business during the final two days. “People are actually more explorative on the weekends,” he said. “They don’t come in with preconceptions of what’s what and what’s worth buying or not.” For an established midsize gallery like his, the public days are a chance to meet collectors who might not already know the artists, or even much about the art market.

Abreu understood the decision to close on Saturday. Sunday was another matter, and sources say exhibitors weren’t consulted before that day was canceled, too. It’s unclear whether or how Art Basel will compensate galleries for closing two days early, though sources tell me a loose coalition of exhibitors is forming to ask the fair for some kind of restitution.

An Art Basel spokesperson said the decision to remain closed Sunday was based on uncertainty about how long the demonstrations might last and their potential impact. The spokesperson said organizers had consulted galleries, the fair’s Selection Committee, and authorities about the early closure, though didn’t specify whether Sunday had been discussed separately. Art Basel is also speaking with exhibitors about possible financial accommodations, but hasn’t announced any measures.

The costs extend beyond the galleries. Art Basel is refunding unused weekend tickets, while restaurants, cabdrivers, and workers at the fair itself lost potential business. Even if every dealer had sold everything by Friday, the financial consequences wouldn’t have stopped at the doors of the Grand Palais.

Cheryl Karim , national fine arts practice leader at the insurance broker Gallagher, has worked in art insurance for some 33 years. She told me that gallery policies can include event-cancellation coverage for documented expenses that can’t be recovered, including booth fees, shipping, storage, and travel. Galleries can also buy separate coverage for individual fairs, although the terms vary considerably.

What can’t be insured is opportunity cost: the possibility that someone might have bought a painting had the fair stayed open. Unlike a conventional retailer, which might be able to show predictable monthly revenue, a gallery can’t easily prove what would have sold on a particular Saturday afternoon. Nor can an insurance policy replace a relationship with a collector who never walked through the door.

Karim said interest in terrorism coverage has increased over the past decade, although insurers have long weighed location, security, transportation, and previous disruptions when evaluating fairs. Clients, she added, are becoming more conscious of what they’re actually buying protection against.

The trouble is that galleries are being asked to take these risks more and more often. A fair can cost tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars before a single work sells. For a smaller business, one disastrous outing can be difficult to recover from. Several in a row can be ruinous.

Art Dubai offers an interesting alternative. After war broke out with Iran on February 28, fair director Dunja Gottweis consulted exhibitors and collectors before postponing the event until May. Galleries could defer until 2027 without additional fees or take part in May without paying booth fees upfront, instead giving organizers a percentage of sales.
“This was really not about making money,” Gottweis told me by phone from Dubai. “This was just to show up and support our community.”

The fair is extending the idea to new exhibitors in 2027, who will pay half their booth fee upfront and the remainder through a percentage of sales. It’s a relatively simple change, but it means organizers share some of the financial risk rather than leaving dealers to shoulder it alone.
But there’s another problem that has nothing to do with protests, natural disasters, or geopolitics: The art world calendar is becoming absurdly crowded.

Philip Hoffman , the art adviser and founder of the Fine Art Group , has grown increasingly frustrated with the relentless string of events. “Right now there are too many fairs crammed into too little time,” he told me. His team has to choose between the November auctions in New York and Frieze Abu Dhabi, which falls during the same period. They’re going to New York.
“I physically can’t get to two places on the same day,” he said.

It’s an obvious limitation, but one the art market seems determined to test. The assumption that collectors, advisers, and galleries can keep adding destinations to their calendars starts to look rather optimistic when even the people with the money and the inclination to travel can’t keep up.

As for geopolitics, Hoffman doesn’t believe instability or civil unrest necessarily discourages collectors from visiting a country, provided they can get in and out safely. The international art market isn’t about to abandon Dubai or Paris because of one difficult year, nor should it.

But Gottweis offered a useful warning to galleries that depend too heavily on a handful of fairs. “It’s dangerous to put all your eggs in one basket and have your business depend on sales during one week. I don’t think the current world is supporting this so much.”
She’s probably right.

None of this means that the art market should stop expanding. Growth outside New York, London, and Switzerland has created opportunities for artists, galleries, and collectors who might otherwise have been left out. Whether that amounts to democratization is another question, especially when the price of admission remains so high.

But an industry that prides itself on its international reach ought to be prepared for the consequences. The world outside the fairgrounds isn’t always peaceful, predictable, or particularly interested in the needs of the art trade. Sometimes it’s at war. Sometimes it’s protesting. Sometimes it’s on fire.

And sometimes, despite all the champagne, business-class flights, hotel suites, and institutional galas, the outside world finds its way inside. The art market wanted to be everywhere. It just hadn’t counted on everything else being there, too.
